examples.before:
.troupe/troupe.yml:
name: demo  # project
? [a, b]
: pair
{x: 1}: flowkey
retry: 3

results.1: exit 4, prints nothing. All three arms report unsupported complex or non-scalar keys, and none gives a line number (e.g. "troupe: complex mapping keys are not supported").
results.2: exit 4, prints nothing. Two arms give the location: "…troupe.yml (line 2, column 3): only scalar mapping keys are supported" and "…mapping key at line 2 under (root) is not a scalar". One arm gives no line: "troupe: error: …troupe.yml: only scalar mapping keys are supported".

results.1: exit 4, same error as above. The file is unchanged and retry stays 3.
results.2: exit 4, same error as above. The file is unchanged and retry stays 3.

context.in_practice: On both routes, every arm refuses the whole file with exit code 4, even for keys that are fine, and never changes the file. The only difference is the error text. On route 2, two of three arms point to line 2. On route 1, no arm gives a line number.
context.stakes: If the config file uses a YAML key that is a list or a map (e.g. `? [a, b]` or `{x: 1}:`), every config command stops working until the user finds and removes that key. What varies is whether the error says where the bad key is.
context.tradeoff: Both routes cost the same: one complex key blocks every config command until it is removed. On route 1 the user also has to find that key without a line number.

plan_why: Loads a troupe.yml with non-scalar mapping keys (a block `? [a, b]` key and a flow `{x: 1}:` key) next to ordinary keys. Route 1 should exit 4 on every command and leave the file alone. An implementation that never considered the case may crash, turn the keys into strings, or load the file, edit it and record history.
